VENIVO is the natural recurrent-background answer after Mentre scrivevo. SONO VENUTO (or VENNI) is also defensible as a completed series of Festival visits during the bounded period when the speaker wrote for that newspaper; sempre does not force the imperfetto.

PASSIAMO is the preferred current-habit answer. PASSEREMO is also defensible if Adesso introduces the team’s current plan for an upcoming June. The month has no year or explicit habitual/future restriction.

DURA is the preferred general-present answer. DURERA is also defensible when the preceding June work is interpreted as a current future plan; the sentence does not independently constrain the tense. The fully accented form is DURERÀ.
CI VEDIAMO is the preferred current routine. CI VEDREMO also works as a planned annual schedule together with PASSEREMO / DURERÀ; February and May are not anchored to a specific year.

MI SVEGLIO is the preferred habitual present. A febbraio, ogni mattina also allows a past February routine (MI SVEGLIAVO) or a future February routine (MI SVEGLIERÒ), if items 7–8 use corresponding tenses. No tense list or year is printed.
MI ALZO is the preferred habitual present. MI ALZAVO or MI ALZERÒ also works coherently with the past/future February interpretations in items 6 and 8.
INIZIO is the preferred habitual present. INIZIAVO or INIZIERÒ also works coherently with the past/future February interpretations in items 6–7.

ANDATE is the preferred general-present comparison. ANDAVATE or ANDRETE can be used with corresponding GUARDAVO or GUARDERÒ in item 10 if the final comparison concerns the past/future February routine. The printed instructions do not restrict tense.

GUARDO is the preferred general-present answer. GUARDAVO or GUARDERÒ gives a coherent past/future work routine when the preceding February sequence and comparison are read in that time frame; no explicit tense constraint rules these out.
